Why is Gaza drowning? Images of floods engulfing Gaza have gone viral. Most coverage focuses on the humanitarian catastrophe. Few explain what caused it. Since October 2023, Israeli forces have destroyed nearly all of Gaza’s infrastructure. Up to 68 million tons of rubble now blanket the Strip. Homes, schools, hospitals, and basic services have been flattened, with at least 90 percent of the territory destroyed. Now, as winter sets in, the first rains are making what is left unlivable. At least five people have been killed after sand embankments collapsed in the downpour. None of this is new. The Israeli plan to make Gaza unlivable has been unfolding for years. In 2012, the UN warned that Gaza could be unlivable by 2020 because of repeated Israeli assaults, a crippling blockade, the collapse of its aquifer, energy shortages, and mass unemployment. Despite the so-called ceasefire, our reporter in Gaza describes a situation that is impossible to endure: no shelter, no aid, and a ban on rebuilding. Conditions are getting worse by the day.” @specter_affairs

Working in coordination with the army and police, nearby settlers wage a ceaseless battle against the Palestinians living in this area. Professor Ilan Pappé describes what has been happening to Masafer Yatta since the 1970’s as “incremental colonization, ethnic cleansing, and oppression,” and to be here is to see it firsthand. But the people of Masafer Yatta have earned a reputation for themselves for their resistance to state and settler terror. They simply refuse to leave, and the Israelis simply won’t stop trying to force them to. The Nakba never ended. We’re just watching its latest act.

A year into the so-called ceasefire, and the occupation’s strikes are still killing Palestinians in Gaza. And as the military occupation continues to restrict the entry of medical supplies, people are also dying preventable deaths because they can’t get the treatment they need. This is manufactured neglect. In October, 42% of essential medicines tracked by Gaza’s Ministry of Health were completely out of stock. The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights reports that more than 350,000 people living with chronic illnesses in Gaza struggle to get their medication. Here, this Hajja from Al-Taqwa Camp in Northern Gaza describes how hard it has been to get treatment and what it meant to have our medical team come to her camp. On September 28, The Sameer Project returned to Al-Taqwa Camp in Sheikh Radwan and saw 42 patients living with conditions including diabetes, high blood pressure, asthma, and atrial fibrillation. We bring care and medication directly to people in displacement camps, and we keep coming back. No one should have to miss a dose because they can’t find or afford their medicine. Patients need to know where their next refill is coming from and who will check on them when their symptoms change. Each mobile Medical Day costs about $700. Donate to The Sameer Project’s Medical Campaign to help us keep bringing lifesaving care and medication to patients who count on our return.
